title: Zona Franca de Manaus: cost estimates
government: Military regime (1967); the extension to 2073 is a later constitutional amendment whose year and government were not verified
what: Tax exemptions for firms in the Manaus Industrial Pole. The Receita's own estimate swings: R$24.2 bn (2021), R$45.59 bn (2022), R$55.26 bn (2023), R$32.7 bn (2024). The effective-base table gives R$25.2 bn for 2021.
who_got: Firms in the pole, whose 2024 turnover was R$204.9 bn: informatics 23.06%, electronics 18.08%, two-wheelers 17.8%. Financed by other taxpayers and, for ICMS, by other states. Federal expenditure flows mostly outside the North.
terms: The dispute is the counterfactual. The Receita counts all PIS, Cofins, IPI and import tax waived. FGV argues the real cost of the industrial pole is only about R$7.5 bn (2021). Industry-only range: R$5.94-9.89 bn potential in 2024 by FGV against the Receita's R$8.74 bn projection. The headline R$22.95 bn (2024, 4.1% of federal expenditure) includes commerce, services and agriculture.
mechanism: Exemption of IPI, import tax, PIS/Cofins and others for firms with approved projects under Suframa (DL 288/1967); constitutional entrenchment (ADCT art. 40) and extension of benefits to 2073 (ADCT art. 92-A). The 1967 decree itself was not opened.
who_paid: The federal budget. FGV says Amazonas returns more federal tax than it receives in benefits (1.74%), and that firms add about R$6.0 bn a year in required counterparts, lifting the Union's return to 2.24%, plus about R$6.0 bn a year of ICMS to the state. FGV's method for the 1.74% was not checked.
after: Constitutional protection to 2073 means no sunset before then. The 2023 tax reform kept the advantage (not confirmed).
counter_view: The FGV report is itself the favourable side: it argues the real cost is lower than the headline. Critics (Senate TD 126 and cost-per-job arguments) say the cost per job is high; the cost per job was not opened.

title: Scale of grilagem: Livro Branco, INCRA 1999/2001 and parliamentary inquiries
government: Medici-era Chamber inquiry (1970); FHC government (1999-2001)
what: Suspected land-grabbing of public land. The 1970 inquiry: Para had the most complaints (17 cases) and 8 million ha sold illegally. Livro Branco (INCRA 1999): about 100 million ha nationwide under suspicion. INCRA 2001 update: 93 million ha, of which Amazonas 55 million ha and Para 31 million ha.
who_got: Large claimants holding forged or inflated titles. INCRA's re-registration of holdings above 10,000 ha cancelled records covering 20 million ha of irregular holdings (Barreto et al. 2008).
terms: Not applicable: appropriation with no price. The public estate was taken for free.
mechanism: Forged titles, inflated areas, registry collusion, later regularization of the occupations.
who_paid: The Union and the states (loss of land); posseiros, Indigenous and traditional peoples (violence).
after: INCRA re-registration, Provimento 13/2006, CNJ cancellations 2009-2010. The 2001 inquiry report is available but was not read in full. A search summary says it cites 'more than 50 million ha' improperly appropriated; not confirmed.
counter_view: 'Area under suspicion' is an estimate, not an adjudicated finding. The 100 million and 93 million figures are not additive with the Para registry totals (different bases and years).

title: North Mato Grosso: private colonizers, Otsar/Cotriguacu and the Sharp episode
government: Medici-Geisel (incentives, SUDAM); Figueiredo
what: INCRA authorised about 36 private colonization firms in northern Mato Grosso. Largest holdings: Rendanyl (later Otsar) 1,000,000 ha; Indeco (Ariosto da Riva) 400,000 ha; Colniza (Lunardelli) 400,000 ha; Juruena (Joao Carlos Meirelles) 200,000 ha. The Otsar land passed to Cotriguacu 'in a fraudulent operation' aimed at a later transfer to the multinational Sharp, the episode that brought down minister Amaury Stabile.
who_got: Colonizers from Parana and Sao Paulo capital and a Parana cooperative (IBGE names the Sao Miguel do Iguacu cooperative; another document names a different one). Fiscal incentives (SUDAM) helped finance them.
terms: Not stated.
mechanism: State land sales to colonizers, grilagem over Indigenous land, then resale or transfer between firms. The one million ha was redistributed as 400,000 ha Cotriguacu, 400,000 ha Juruena and 200,000 ha Indeco.
who_paid: Indigenous peoples, posseiros, and the public estate. Only Indeco implemented its colonization on time; the others did little and the land did not return to the public estate.
after: Colonizers sold lots to settlers from the South. A named 'Fazenda Cotriguacu' grilagem case was NOT found; only the colonizer is documented.
counter_view: Colonizers describe themselves as 'Bandeirantes of the 20th century', building towns on empty land (Travessia quotes this self-image).

title: State takeover (estatizacao) of the private external debt
government: Geisel and Figueiredo (military regime); Delfim Netto at planning/finance
what: Private and state-firm foreign debts under Lei 4.131 and Resolucao 63 loans were taken onto the public side. No single headline figure for the private-then-public share could be quoted safely; the two papers give series.
who_got: Private Brazilian borrowers and state firms were relieved of dollar risk. The foreign creditor banks were made whole through the 1982 rescheduling backed by the IMF.
terms: The central bank sold exchange cover below the cost of the later devaluations (Cruz 1995).
mechanism: Central bank and CMN circulars and resolutions, not laws passed by Congress: Circular 230/1974 and Resolucao 432/1977 (the BC guaranteed the exchange rate on foreign loans), DRME deposits, and project deposits so that private debtors paid cruzeiros to the BC while the BC owed the creditors dollars.
who_paid: The Treasury and the central bank (money printing, internal debt), so inflation and the lost decade fell on wage earners.
after: The debt was later converted into the Brady bonds of 1994 (not opened).
counter_view: The state took the debt to avoid a wave of private bankruptcies and a payments default during the 1982 crisis (argued in the IPEA text).

title: Carlos Medeiros, the 'phantom landowner' of Para

title: PROER: the Nacional, Economico and Bamerindus operations
government: Fernando Henrique Cardoso; BC presidents Gustavo Loyola, with Gustavo Franco as BC director (who signed which operation not confirmed)
what: Federal credit to buyer banks taking over failed banks (MP 1.179 and 1.182 of Nov 1995, CMN Res. 2.208). The Chamber inquiry report says R$20.4 bn lent and R$7.1 bn net loss to the Union around 2002.
who_got: The BC lent to the buyer bank; Itau-type buyers took Economico's good assets, Unibanco took Nacional's, HSBC took Bamerindus in March 1997 (date from snippet). Healthy assets went to the buyer; bad assets and housing-fund (FCVS) credits stayed in the liquidated estate. The Union financed it through BC credit and bond sterilisation.
terms: The loans were at below-market terms and long maturities (inquiry chapter VI). At Nacional the hole was hidden by fictitious loans for years.
mechanism: MPs 1.179/1.182 and CMN Res. 2.208. Lei 9.447/97 later made controllers jointly liable and allowed their assets to be frozen.
who_paid: The Treasury, through BC provisions that flow into its balance. Controllers largely kept personal wealth, hence decades-long collection fights.
after: The Proer inquiry concluded intervention was necessary but criticised controls; the BC attorney-general argued losses of R$40 bn or R$69.5 bn were avoided (exact attribution to be re-checked). FGC and the sale of the estates continued into the 2020s.
counter_view: A systemic run in 1995 would have cost more; supporters point to avoided losses of R$40 bn or R$69.5 bn (BC attorney-general, cited in the inquiry chapter; attribution to be re-checked).

title: Lei Kandir: ICMS exemption on exports of primary goods
government: Fernando Henrique Cardoso government (signatory not confirmed from an opened page); the compensation fight ran under every later government
what: The state tax ICMS was waived on exports of primary and semi-finished goods (LC 87, 13 Sept 1996). Loss estimates differ: R$268.9 bn accumulated 1997-2016 (R$25 bn in 2016 alone) versus R$637 bn since 1996 as of 2019.
who_got: Exporters of ore, soy, meat, pulp and similar goods (named companies not opened). Financed by states and municipalities. By 2016 the biggest absolute losses were Minas Gerais R$64.6 bn, Rio R$60.7 bn, Para R$35.7 bn, Mato Grosso R$30.8 bn, Espirito Santo R$28.3 bn. As a share of revenue: Mato Grosso 26.01%, Para 14.58%.
terms: Compensation to states was never based on measured loss. The STF found Congress had failed to regulate ADCT art. 91 for more than ten years after EC 42/2003.
mechanism: LC 87/1996 art. 3 exemption; transitional compensation in art. 31 and annex, amended by LC 115/2002; EC 42/2003 wrote the exemption into the Constitution and created ADCT art. 91. ADO 25 was filed in 2013 by Para and 15 other states (rapporteur Gilmar Mendes). On 30 Nov 2016 the STF unanimously found the omission and gave Congress 12 months; the TCU would set the amount if Congress failed.
who_paid: The states. LC 176/2020 pays R$58 bn from 2020 to 2037: R$4 bn a year to 2030 (R$1 bn to municipalities), then falling R$500 mn a year for 2031-2037. Extra R$7.6 bn brings the total to R$65.6 bn. States had to drop lawsuits against the Union to receive it.
after: The R$58 bn is far below either loss estimate, so on those numbers the settlement repays a fraction. Whether the exemption brought more exports than it cost is not documented.
counter_view: The Union argued it already transfers large sums to states and that the temporary scheme is constitutional (Conjur, 13 Dec 2016). The rapporteur replied that social contributions, which are not shared with states, rose from 29% to 54% of federal revenue between 1994 and 2016. A Folha Vitoria headline says the Fazenda held that the law does not oblige full repayment; that page returned 403 and was not read. The economic defence (exports and the trade balance rose) is not documented.

title: Dividend tax exemption
government: FHC (law of 26 Dec 1995, date from a URL slug); Lula III for Lei 15.270/2025
what: Profits distributed to owners escaped personal income tax from January 1996. Ipea (Gobetti and Orair) estimated in 2015 that a 15% tax on profits and dividends would raise R$43 bn a year (R$50 bn in another version).
who_got: Owners and shareholders of companies. 71,440 Brazilians earning over R$1.3 million a year declared an average of R$4.2 million and paid 6.7% in tax. A senator compared a civil servant paying 27.5% on R$5,000 with an owner receiving R$300,000 in dividends paying nothing. Financed by employees and consumers through payroll and consumption taxes.
terms: Ipea estimate of revenue forgone. The claim that 'only Brazil and Estonia fully exempt dividends' is a senator's hearing statement; a search did not confirm Estonia. An OECD comparison was not opened.
mechanism: Art. 10 of Lei 9.249/1995 exempts distributed profits from withholding and from the recipient's tax base. The same law's art. 9 created interest on equity (JCP), deductible from corporate tax (text not opened). Lei 15.270/2025: 10% withholding when a company pays one resident individual over R$50,000 a month; non-residents pay 10%; a minimum tax starts at R$600,000 a year and reaches 10% at R$1.2 million.
who_paid: Wage earners (labour income taxed up to 27.5%) and the Treasury.
after: After about 30 years, Lei 15.270/2025 reintroduced a withholding, effective 1 Jan 2026 (date from a snippet). Dividends from profits up to fiscal year 2025 stay exempt.
counter_view: The defence reported by IHU is that the exemption avoids taxing profit twice, at the company and again as personal income. The opposing argument, that the 1995 corporate rate cut and the JCP deduction already lower the corporate burden, was not sourced.

title: PROES and Banespa
government: Fernando Henrique Cardoso
what: The Union issued federal securities to states to clean up state banks (MP 1.514/1996, CMN Res. 2.365/1997) and refinanced state debts (Lei 9.496/97). Banespa was federalised in Dec 1994 and sold to Santander in Nov 2000. The BCB book counts R$61.4 bn in securities issued under PROES.

title: Oil royalties and the special participation
government: Military regime (1969), Sarney (1989), FHC (1997), Lula (2010), Dilma (2012); signatories not verified
what: The question is how much of the oil rent the state kept. Lei 9.478/1997 raised the basic royalty from 5% to up to 10% (snippet only); the ANP says the field rate can vary from 5% to 15% by contract. Royalties plus special participation grew 5,204% from 1999 to 2025 and in 2022 first exceeded ICMS on fuel. The TCU reports R$58.22 bn paid in 2024.
who_got: The state kept more as production rose. Distribution is concentrated: ten municipalities hold half of the municipal share and have under 9 million people; some get over R$20,000 per resident per year. Lei 12.734 cut the 'confronting states' share from about 30% to 20% and 'confronting municipalities' from 20% to 4%.
terms: In the concession regime the rent is split by rate, not by auction price alone. Bonus, royalty and special participation by field were not opened. In 1997 the 5% rate produced only about R$208 million in today's values.
mechanism: Concession contracts (Lei 9.478/1997); production sharing in the pre-salt (Lei 12.351/2010); redistribution under Lei 12.734/2012. The STF suspended the redistribution rules in 2013 (ADI 4917), with the final status not confirmed.
who_paid: Non-producing states and municipalities under the old distribution; producing ones after Lei 12.734 if it takes effect. The TCU found weaknesses in how the ANP calculates and distributes.
after: More revenue as production rose 61% between 2015 and 2025 and prices moved. The ANP projects R$68 bn for 2025. The Petrobras corruption context is in other notes.

title: Repetro: customs regime for oil and gas equipment
government: FHC (1999) and Temer (2017) by date in office; the sources do not name the president
what: Relief from import tax, IPI, PIS and Cofins on equipment for oil and gas exploration. INESC crossed Receita data with the 267 firms listed under Repetro: R$260.08 bn of incentives, exemptions and immunities in 2015-2023.
who_got: Most of the 267 firms are transnationals; the top three include MODEC and Ventura Petroleo. Petrobras-operated fields produce 88-89% of Brazilian oil, so some benefit reaches Petrobras. Financed by the Treasury.
terms: The Receita says it is technically impossible to compute Repetro as a deviation from the reference system, so it is not in the official tax expenditure report. INESC says the Receita holds robust data and could publish it.
mechanism: Special customs regime: suspension of II, IPI, PIS/Pasep and Cofins on goods for oil, gas and hydrocarbon activities, becoming exemption or zero rate once used as required. Decreto 3.161/1999; Lei 12.276/2010 and 12.351/2010 (pre-salt); Lei 13.586/2017 extended it to 31 Dec 2040. LC 215/2025 kept it among relieved regimes.
who_paid: The federal budget.
after: INESC says values grew significantly from 2017, though the table peaks in 2020 and declines to 2022, so the table alone does not prove cause.
counter_view: The regime is defended as a way to avoid taxing imported capital goods that would be re-exported (position not documented in an opened page). The Receita's own treatment, that Repetro is not a deviation from the reference system, is the verified form of the same argument.

title: REFIS and tax amnesties (special instalment programs)
government: FHC (Refis 2000), Lula (Paes 2003, Paex 2006, Refis da Crise 2009), Dilma (reopenings), Temer (Pert 2017); signatories not in the TCU chart
what: Repeated special instalment programs for tax debts. The TCU counts about 28 programs in 2000-2017; the Receita counts about 40 in 18 years costing R$176 bn. Pert forgave R$47.4 bn and Refis da Crise R$60.9 bn.
who_got: Debtors, including large firms; named beneficiaries not in the opened pages. Pert covered 131 thousand taxpayers. Taxpayers who joined three or more programs owed over R$160 bn and about half defaulted afterwards. Financed by compliant taxpayers and the social security budget.
terms: The TCU says the payment terms 'find no parallel in the world'. Pert gave discounts up to 70% off fines and 90% off interest, and up to 175 instalments. The exact month counts in the TCU comparison chart were not extractable.
mechanism: Each program is a medida provisoria converted into law, with discounts on fines and interest and long instalment plans. Lei 9.964/2000 (from MP 2.004-6/2000) created the first Refis; Paes 2003 is Lei 10.684/2003; Refis da Crise is Lei 11.941/2009.
who_paid: The Treasury and social security funds. The TCU argues repeated amnesties reward non-payment and punish those who paid on time. The Pert and Refis da Crise forgiveness sums to R$108.3 bn (my sum from press figures); it overlaps with the Receita's R$176 bn and cannot be added.
after: More programs followed after 2017, including 2020-2021 transaction regimes (not confirmed). Refis 2000 amounts were not opened.
counter_view: The usual defence is that a collectible stream beats an uncollectible stock (no page opened to source it). The Receita itself is quoted as opposing a new Refis (Netcpa), so the tax authority does not back the practice.

title: Para registry with more land than the state, and the CNJ cancellations
government: Lula government; the Judiciary (CNJ, TJ-PA Corregedoria, with Iterpa and INCRA)
what: CNJ-driven cancellations hit at least 10,728 registrations in 88 municipalities covering 91.1 million ha in Para. Separately, one registration of 410 million ha in the Vitoria do Xingu registry was cancelled in 2009, '3.9 times the size of Para'.
who_got: Claimants through 'phantom' owners and fake inventories; the people behind most chains are not identified. Where later sold, buyers were logging and cattle interests.
terms: No price; purchases were mostly registry entries.
mechanism: Duplicated or inflated registrations, forged adjudication letters, notary collusion. Lei 6.739/1979 allowed administrative cancellation of null registrations; Provimento 13/2006 blocked registrations by size and date criteria. TJ-PA ordered only blocks, so the matter went to CNJ.
who_paid: The state and the Union (land lost, years of litigation); innocent third-party buyers when registrations were cancelled.

counter_view: The cancellations were administrative and based on size and date proxies, so some legitimate titles may have been caught; critics call it a legal-certainty problem (a jus.com.br article, listed in search and not read).

title: Federal tax expenditures (gastos tributarios) series
government: Lula II, Dilma, Temer, Bolsonaro, Lula III (the series grows under all of them)
what: Revenue not collected through exemptions, deductions, reduced rates and deferrals. In the Receita Federal series it rose from R$114.8 bn (3.82% of GDP) in 2008 to R$519.0 bn (4.78%) in 2023. The 2024 value of R$512.3 bn is a projection.
who_got: In 2021: Simples Nacional 21.70% (R$91.3 bn), agriculture and agroindustry 12.12%, exempt personal income 8.85%, regional development 7.91%, non-profits 7.56%. Manaus and free-trade areas got R$25.2 bn (5.98%). 62% of federal tax expenditure flows to the Southeast and South. Financed by all other taxpayers.
terms: The figure is the Receita's own estimate, not a market valuation. It leaves out several large items (Repetro, dividends, interest on equity, presumed profit) because the reference system treats them as normal or too hard to compute. So it is a floor, not a ceiling.
mechanism: Hundreds of separate norms: Simples (LC 123/2006), PIS/COFINS zero rates, income tax exemptions, regional regimes. The legal basis of the report itself was not opened. Portaria RFB 319 (2023) and LC 187/2021 allowed publishing beneficiaries by company.
who_paid: Other taxpayers. In 2021 federal expenditure equalled 24.03% of federal collection. FGV IBRE puts state expenditures at 2.4% of GDP in 2024, so federal plus state may reach 7.2% of GDP.
after: The 2024 tax reform (EC 132/2023) and later proposals targeted tax expenditures (not confirmed from an opened page). The report still excludes the largest special regimes.
counter_view: Brazil is not an outlier. For 2021 the Receita table puts Brazil at 4.67% of GDP against a Latin American listing average of 5.26%; Canada 7.94%, US 6.06%, Colombia 7.73%, Chile 2.49%, Peru 1.82%. The Receita notes each country uses its own method. FGV says Brazil's 2002-2022 average was 3.0% of GDP against Italy 7.0% and US 6.9%. The dispute is about the pace of growth and who benefits (Receita Federal DGT; FGV EESP report).

title: Terra Legal: prices charged versus market value, and the TCU audits
government: Lula (2009); Temer (2017 changes); Bolsonaro (MP 910/2019); also state governments (Para, Amapa, Roraima)
what: Federal titling of occupied public land in the Amazon. Imazon: privatising the 19.6 million ha of undesignated federal land at current legal values would cost society R$62-88 billion, about a quarter of Petrobras's 2019 market value. In Para the gap between market value and state price reaches R$9 billion across 8,053 properties.
who_got: Occupants of federal land in the Amazon, including holders above the legal limit. TCU audited R$58.6 billion of land; 62 holders above 2,500 ha occupy 540 thousand ha.
terms: Lei 11.952 art. 11: free titling up to 1 fiscal module; art. 12: larger areas at 10% to 50% of the INCRA minimum land-value table, paid over 20 years with up to 3 years of grace. That table is itself below market. Amapa sold areas for as little as 4% of market value and Roraima allowed up to 85% discount for those who deforested (both search summaries).
mechanism: Dispensation of bidding; discounts by size; instalments; self-declared occupation with remote checks. State land agencies (Iterpa in Para, and in Amapa and Roraima) used discounted price tables; Roraima Lei 976/2014 as changed by Lei 1.351/2019.
who_paid: The Treasury (forgone revenue), state treasuries, the forest, and legitimate small occupants who wait.
after: The TCU ordered recovery of irregular areas; no complete recovery was found. TCU 627/2015 price findings not confirmed. Title production fell to almost zero in the first half of 2019.
counter_view: The government argued the subsidy helps poor occupants and low land values reflect poor access and lack of infrastructure. Imazon replies that most area goes to large claimants and that the subsidy brings no socioenvironmental return (Imazon, 10 facts).

title: Undesignated public forests and CAR self-declarations
government: Dilma (CAR created with the Forest Code 2012); Temer and Bolsonaro (registrations rose)
what: Undesignated public forests cover 57.5 million ha in the Amazon. By 2020, 18.6 million ha of them (32%) were illegally registered in the rural environmental registry (CAR). Imazon counts 86.1 million ha (17% of the Amazon) still awaiting a destination.

title: CFEM mining royalty and the 2017 reform
government: Michel Temer (2017 reform)
what: The public share of mineral rent. Before 2017 the royalty was charged on net revenue: iron ore 2%, gold 1%, bauxite/manganese/potassium 3%, precious stones 0.2%. Collection was R$7.45 bn in 2024 on R$270.8 bn of mineral operations; iron ore supplied 75.01% of it.
who_got: Miners keep the rent after the royalty. Petrobras plus mining make up 51.2% of 18 'super-profit' companies listed in the slides (profit year not stated). Company-level payments were not extracted. Financed by producing municipalities and the public that bears the environmental cost.
terms: Lei 13.540/2017 moved the base from net to gross revenue less sale taxes, and raised the iron ore ceiling from 2% to 3.5% (can be cut to 2%), gold 1% to 1.5%, diamond 0.2% to 2%, niobium 2% to 3%. Other systems tax margin or profit: Ontario 10% of net profit, Quebec 12%, Newfoundland 16%, Peru 1-12% of operating profit, Chile 1% of sales plus 8-26% of operating margin, South Africa 0.5-7%, Western Australia 7.5% of sales on iron ore (official page not opened).
mechanism: Lei 13.540/2017 (from MP 789/2017). Old distribution: 12% Union, 23% state, 65% producing municipality, with a 50% landowner share under Lei 8.901/94. The pre-2017 net base let firms shrink the amount due.
who_paid: Public revenue lost to under-payment. The TCU found about 69.7% of titleholders did not pay voluntarily in 2017-2022, and those who paid under-reported by 40.2% on average (cited by industry lawyers; the TCU PDF itself was unreadable). Lawyers estimate better enforcement could lift collection to about R$16 bn with no rate change.
after: Collection grew about fourfold between 2017 and 2024, but how much comes from the new base versus price and volume is not separated. A Chamber hearing on 12 Aug 2025 shows the fight is still open.
counter_view: The industry side (Eixos, by FPA Advocacia) says nominal rates cannot be compared across regimes, a rate on gross revenue can be as onerous as higher rates elsewhere, and the problem is enforcement not rate. The opposite view (Giliad slides to the Chamber) frames sector profitability as the base for a higher take. The effective-rate comparison could not be settled from the pages opened.
